According to experts at the watchdog Environmental Working Group (2018), the government's levels of allowable pesticides are too liberal. They agree, however, that the health benefits of eating more fruits and vegetables outweigh the known risks of consuming pesticide residue. So what's a hungry, but poor, athlete to do? © Eat a variety of foods to minimize exposure to a specific pesticide residue. © Carefully wash and rinse fruits and vegetables under running water; this can remove 99 percent of pesticide residue (depending on the food and the pesticide). Building a High-Energy Eating Plan 31 * Peel foods such as apples, potatoes, carrots, and pears (but keep in mind that this also peels off important nutrients). * Remove the tops and outer portions of celery, lettuce, and cabbage. © Buy organic versions of the foods you eat most often, such as apples if you are a five-a-day apple eater. © When buying the fruits and vegetables that are known to have the highest amounts of pesticide residue (although they are still within the EPA’s limits), choose organic: strawberries, spinach, nectarines, apples, grapes, peaches, cherries, pears, tomatoes, celery, potatoes, and bell peppers. * To save money, choose conventionally grown fruits and vegetables known to have little or no pesticide residue (or nonedible skins that will be removed): avocado, sweet corn, pineapple, cabbage, onion, frozen sweet peas, papaya, asparagus, mango, eggplant, honeydew melon, kiwi, cantaloupe, cauliflower, and broccoli. | ey ~ /- b 7 Sey 5 wy A 7 QD | J
